query: For high-entropy-alloy protective coatings in wear-resistant applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their wear performance and why? Define a controlled change that would distinguish the hypothesis from a baseline, the directional observations expected if it is correct, the range over which it should hold, the prior evidence that supports it, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The excellent wear performance of high-entropy alloy coatings is governed by the in situ formation of an ultra‐nanocrystalline (or reactive oxide nanocomposite) surface layer under friction, which distributes stresses and accommodates plastic deformation, thereby reducing friction and wear.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-sprayed high-entropy alloy protective coating with a mixed microstructure that includes fine (nanocrystalline) and coarser grains.
generation.intervention: A controlled pre-wear modification that coarsens the initial grain structure (for example, via a low-temperature annealing treatment) to reduce the coating’s predisposition to form the dynamic nanolayer during wear.
generation.conditions: Dry sliding wear tests at room temperature under a fixed normal load in an inert or controlled ambient where oxidation is limited.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a wear-induced ultra-nanocrystalline (or oxide nanocomposite) surface layer that appears at the frictional interface.
generation.mechanism: Under mechanical shear during sliding, strain localization drives either dynamic amorphization or limited reactive oxidation that refines the near-surface grain structure. This transformation creates a finely grained layer that distributes stress more evenly and allows for multiple deformation pathways, resulting in a lower friction coefficient and reduced material loss.
generation.predicted_outcome: When the as-sprayed coatings (with a fine initial microstructure) are subjected to wear, they will rapidly develop a protective nanolayer, exhibit lower friction coefficients and significantly reduced wear rates compared to coatings that have been pre-annealed to coarsen the microstructure. The effect should be observable under the applied wear conditions over the typical load and time scales used in such studies.
generation.baseline: The unmodified (as-sprayed) HEA coating that naturally forms the nanolayer during wear.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to govern wear performance under moderate to high sliding loads and at ambient temperature (or conditions where the kinetics are sufficient to allow dynamic nanolayer formation). The effect may be limited if wear conditions (e.g., speed, temperature) do not allow for sufficient interface transformation.
generation.uncertainty: It remains uncertain whether the protective nanolayer forms primarily via mechanically induced amorphization or through a limited reactive oxidation process, and how sensitive this mechanism is to the specific alloy composition and testing environment.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA coatings: one in the as-sprayed (fine-grained) state and one that has been pre-annealed to coarsen the grain structure. Subject both sets to identical dry sliding wear tests under controlled ambient conditions. Use high-resolution microscopy (e.g., TEM) and surface analysis (e.g., XRD) to characterize the wear interface after testing.
measurements: Wear rate (volume loss per unit load and distance)
Grain size and phase structure at the worn surface (via TEM/XRD)
Surface composition if oxidation is implicated
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If both the as-sprayed and annealed coatings display similar wear performance and show comparable formation (or absence) of a protective ultra-nanocrystalline or reactive oxide nanocomposite surface layer, then the hypothesis that the dynamic formation of this layer governs the improved wear performance is disproven.

Remarkable Wear Resistance in a Complex Concentrated Alloy with Nanohierarchical Architecture and Composition Undulation

Abstract: AbstractSustained wear damages on the sliding surfaces of alloys are generally the culprit responsible for the failure of various mechanical systems. Inspired by high-entropy effects, here we deliberately deploy nanohierarchical architecture with composition undulation in a Ni50(AlNbTiV)50 complex concentrated alloy, which yields ultralow wear rate within the order of 10−7 to 10−6 mm3/Nm between room temperature and 800 °C. Such remarkable wear resistance heretofore represents one of the highest wear resistance reported for the bulk alloys or composites, and originates from the multi-type adaptive friction interface protection governed by intrinsically nano-coupled grains and nanoprecipitates. This cooperative heterostructure releases gradient frictional stress in stages upon wear at room temperature through the coexistence of multiple deformation pathways while activating a dense nanocrystalline glaze layer upon wear at 800 °C to minimize adhesive and oxidative wear. Microstructural Evolution of AlCoCrFeNiSi High-Entropy Alloy Powder during Mechanical Alloying and Its Coating Performance

Abstract: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) are promising structural materials due to their excellent comprehensive performances. The use of mechanically alloyed powders to deposit HEA coatings through atmospheric plasma spraying (APS) is an effective approach that can broaden the application areas of the HEAs. In this paper, a ductility–brittleness AlCoCrFeNiSi system was chosen as an object of study, and the detailed evolution of the surface morphology, particle size distribution, and microstructure of the powder during mechanical alloying was investigated. An AlCoCrFeNiSi HEA coating was deposited using powder milled for 10 h, which can be used as an ideal feedstock for APS. The surface morphology, microstructure, microhardness, and wear behavior of the coating at room temperature were investigated. The results showed that as the milling time increased, the particle size first increased, and then decreased. Synthesis and Mechanical Characterization of a CuMoTaWV High-Entropy Film by Magnetron Sputtering

Abstract: Development of high-entropy alloy (HEA) films is a promising and cost-effective way to incorporate these materials of superior properties in harsh environments. In this work, a refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) film of equimolar CuMoTaWV was deposited on silicon and 304 stainless-steel substrates using DC-magnetron sputtering. A sputtering target was developed by partial sintering of an equimolar powder mixture of Cu, Mo, Ta, W, and V using spark plasma sintering. The target was used to sputter a nanocrystalline RHEA film with a thickness of ∼900 nm and an average grain size of 18 nm. X-ray diffraction of the film revealed a body-centered cubic solid solution with preferred orientation in the (110) directional plane. The nanocrystalline nature of the RHEA film resulted in a hardness of 19 ± 2.3 GPa and an elastic modulus of 259 ± 19.2 GPa. A high compressive strength of 10 ± 0.8 GPa was obtained in nanopillar compression due to solid solution hardening and grain boundary strengthening. Evidence of Inverse Hall-Petch Behavior and Low Friction and Wear in High Entropy Alloys

Abstract: AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2).
